classification.difficultyReason: Inspect each supplied graph for y-axis reflection symmetry and origin half-turn symmetry, then assign even, odd or neither without algebraic calculation.

content.prompt: Classify each function $y=f(x)$ as odd, even or neither.

spec.description: Unscaled increasing S-shaped sketch with a horizontal flattening point on the y-axis below the origin and a positive x-intercept. No numerical ticks or grid. Black axes and curve.
spec.mathematics: The curve lacks both y-axis symmetry and origin symmetry. Bézier segments preserve the qualitative source sketch without asserting an equation or numerical coordinates.
spec.answerVisibility: The supplied graph is visible in all editions; the classification is answer-only.

answer.worked: The graph has neither reflection symmetry about the $y$-axis nor rotational symmetry of $180^\circ$ about the origin. The function is neither even nor odd.

spec.description: Unscaled cubic-shaped sketch passing through the origin, with opposite local maximum and minimum, three x-intercepts, and arrows down-left and up-right. Labelled axes, no numerical ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: Exact origin symmetry is preserved by centrally reflected Bézier control points. The sketch does not assert a numerical function rule.
spec.answerVisibility: The supplied graph is visible in all editions; the classification is answer-only.

answer.worked: The graph has rotational symmetry of $180^\circ$ about the origin, so $f(-x)=-f(x)$. The function is odd.

spec.description: Upward-opening parabola with its vertex on the y-axis below the origin, equal-height arrowed ends and symmetric x-intercepts. Axes labelled x and y; no numerical ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: An unscaled parabolic representative preserves the source's y-axis symmetry and vertex/intercept relationships. Internal drawing coordinates are not student givens.
spec.answerVisibility: The supplied graph is visible in all editions; the classification is answer-only.

answer.worked: The graph has reflection symmetry about the $y$-axis, so $f(-x)=f(x)$. The function is even.
